title: I learned manifestation at Stanford
summary: A hosts-only Season 3 bonus episode on mental well-being, covering therapy, spiritual health, mantras and antidepressants. Cherie and Jean share their own therapy histories, how to 'date' therapists, CBT versus talk therapy, how to budget for sessions, and the four mantras Cherie learned from Stanford professor Joel Peterson that now appear on the Sisters Matcha can.

ideas.idea: What got you here will not get you to the next level; ambitious type-A people must invest in mental health as much as physical health.
ideas.detail: The hosts frame therapy, spiritual health and mantras as the mental counterpart to the diet and exercise discussed in their previous episode, arguably just as important for a healthy, wealthy, joyful life.

ideas.idea: Therapy is transformative because you go in with one presenting problem and end up unpacking upbringing, family and career.
ideas.detail: Cherie first used free campus counseling in college during a hard sophomore year and a senior-year breakup, then returned in 2019 as a new grad over a romantic issue and went consistently for a year; she says she is who she is today because of that work.

ideas.idea: 'Therapist dating' is real: you will not click with every therapist, so try several until you find one whose demeanor, background and method fit you.
ideas.detail: Jean switched away from a college therapist because she felt unable to discuss body-image distress with someone who was obese, and a male friend avoided an Asian woman therapist because it felt too much like talking to his mom. Jean found her archetype, an older gay man using CBT in NYC around 2011, and has sought that type in every city since.

ideas.idea: Therapy is not a walk in the park; it is the mental equivalent of a gym workout that builds emotional muscle and breaks old patterns of thinking.
ideas.detail: Cherie says it is the hardest and best thing she has ever done because confronting your own bad and good parts is terrifying; Jean compares it to changing how you have moved your body every day of your life. You can set expectations to ease in and build rapport before tackling the deepest issues.

ideas.idea: Once experienced with therapy, walk in with your own agenda for the session so you know what you want to get out of it.
ideas.detail: Cherie tells her therapist which topics she wants to cover and treats leaving in tears as a sign she is working through something; a college therapist who was a Black woman also taught her the concept of intersectionality, showing therapy can be academic and growth-oriented.

ideas.idea: Use your health insurance for therapy whenever you can, because out-of-pocket sessions run $300-$400 for 45-50 minutes.
ideas.detail: Cherie paid $10 per session on LinkedIn's insurance and now pays far more without it but still considers it worth it; Jean always stayed in-network, which made finding a new therapist after job or insurance changes a burden since in-network therapists are often not taking new patients. A friend in 2011 already paid $350 a session.

ideas.idea: Pre-allocate a fixed annual budget for therapy, like a friend's $10,000 a year, so you do the worrying up front and never agonize over each session.
ideas.detail: Cherie's friend treats the $10,000 as the price of his mental health and skips a vacation instead; the hosts generalize this to any major expense, which requires a good handle on your overall budget.

ideas.idea: Cognitive behavioral therapy beats plain talk therapy because it gives you evergreen tools and frameworks you can use in real time for the rest of your life.
ideas.detail: Jean prefers directive therapists who assign homework and cite studies over the movie-style 'how did that make you feel'; she wants the PhD to share the knowledge rather than ask what she thinks. Cherie, by contrast, has only done talk therapy and developed her own bespoke frameworks and pattern recognition.

ideas.idea: To stop catastrophizing, project the scenario forward and name the best case, the worst case and the most likely case, which drains the power of 'what if'.
ideas.detail: A CBT technique Jean learned over ten years ago and still applies; you realize the outcome will probably be middle of the road rather than either extreme.

ideas.idea: EMDR (eye movement desensitization and reprocessing) is another option that combines talk therapy with eye movements to process trauma.
ideas.detail: Jean initially thought it sounded like a bit much, but a girlfriend who loves it and found it hugely helpful opened her mind to trying different modalities.

ideas.idea: Spiritual health means feeling connected to something larger than yourself, and it is a spectrum from faith to mantras and manifesting that need not involve religion.
ideas.detail: Jean finds faith most beautiful when it is a one-on-one relationship with God divorced from an institution, and dislikes religion used as an excuse for bad behavior; Cherie prays daily for wisdom and patience and jokes that God then sends tests of both.

ideas.idea: Build mantras by taking your biggest insecurity and flipping it into its positive opposite, then repeat it to rewire your brain's operating system.
ideas.detail: Stanford GSB professor Joel Peterson, now 77, derived his mantras from where he struggled most: 'It's not about me' to counter self-centeredness at the height of his career, 'I am not my emotions' because he ran hot, plus 'I have everything I need' and 'I am grateful'. Cherie copied all four and writes them in her journal repeatedly whenever she feels overwhelmed until she feels centered.

ideas.idea: 'I have everything I need' is printed on top of every Sisters Matcha can as a daily mantra to say while preparing the matcha.
ideas.detail: The hosts chose the Peterson mantra as their brand's message; Jean notes repeating a mantra is functionally similar to standardized prayers asking for patience and grace.

ideas.idea: There should be zero stigma around antidepressants and SSRIs; they are a viable path to getting better.
ideas.detail: Multiple girlfriends recently told Jean they are on SSRIs with no fanfare, and the conversations carried no shame; you need not announce it, but know it is available and talk to a medical professional.

ideas.idea: Having means to pay is not the same as willingness to pay; each person must decide their own price for mental health.
ideas.detail: It feels weird to put a price on mental health, but Cherie went from $10 copays to full price and still chooses to invest in it, while friends pay $350-$400 per session out of pocket.
